While the possibility of tank rupture was considered, composite hydrogen onboard tanks typically have a burst pressure which is 2.1 times the maximum operating pressure [5]. Furthermore, these tanks feature TPRDs, which open at a set maximum temperature or pressure to release the contents of a tank to preserve its integrity, making rupture less likely. Rail cars undergo unique shock and vibration conditions compared to other vehicles, such as ~2 g during shock events and between 22-26 g during rail coupling, with loading and unloading on the transport platform as one of the greatest contributors to stress [16, 17]. To account for this, the loosening of connections was considered in this analysis, along with the loosening or expansion of components due to exterior washing and repeated fueling and defueling. Circumstances where hydrogen could become trapped in overhead or ceiling spaces, including within enclosed maintenance pits with solid or canopy ceilings, were also considered. In rail maintenance facilities there may be heat or spark sources from welding or heavy metal-on-metal work such as from brake repair, roller bearing replacement, wheel/bogie replacement, valve testing 12 and repair, dent or panel welding, and/or train car coupler replacement [18]. Likewise, there may be significant tooling of parts occurring near the rail car such as lathe wheel turning, milling, boring, grinding, planing, and cutting [19]. Since substantial heat or spark sources coincident with accumulated flammable hydrogen may present a greater likelihood of hazardous conditions for workers and equipment, this type of condition was included in this analysis. Additionally, hot work operations can loosen or expand connections which may start as small leaks and lead to loss of hydrogen during use or service. Since hot work can also promote high temperature hydrogen attack (HTHA) of materials which can compromise the integrity of steel components, hazards associated with this type of service activity were also included [20]. Additional sources of heat which may come from potential on-site fires started from chemicals such as aerosols, brake cleaner, degreaser, part cleaner, lubricants, paint, interior/exterior cleaning solvents and rags typically used in rail maintenance were also considered [19] which, if improperly stored, may create a fire which can increase the likelihood of a TPRD opening and release the contents of a hydrogen tank. Based on analysis from hydrogen incidents [12, 13], other aspects of maintenance that we considered included material and procedural failures. The use of incompatible materials as well as corrosion of components not detected during inspection or prevented from maintenance were examined. Additionally, fuel systems not being purged or defueled properly, including accidental venting indoors due to poor interconnections, inappropriate ventilation, or poor gas detection were considered. TPRDs not opening or venting due to fatigue of components, icing causing blockage and over-pressurization, or inadequate design and/or installation were also important scenarios explored.
